title: Nickelodeon:The Best of Slimes
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) trace the history of Nickelodeon from its 1977 start as a Warner Cable test in Columbus, Ohio, through its Pinwheel roots, the 1979 rename, the Cy Schneider and Geraldine Laybourne eras, its slime and game shows (You Can't Do That on Television, Double Dare), Nick at Night, the cartoon boom (Ren and Stimpy, Rugrats, SpongeBob SquarePants), and the later decline. The episode includes a content warning and substantial discussion of child sexual abuse and misconduct at the network tied to Dan Schneider, John Kricfalusi, Brian Peck, and others, plus Jeanette McCurdy's allegations, the documentary Quiet on the Set, and a listener mail segment about nautical terms (rope vs. line).
topics: You Can't Do That on Television
listener mail nautical rope vs line

entities.name: You Can't Do That on Television

segments.title: Content warning and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, with a content warning that the Nickelodeon history includes sexual abuse, and reminisce about watching Nickelodeon as kids.

segments.title: Warner Cable Columbus test and Pinwheel origins
segments.summary: Nickelodeon began in 1977 as part of a Warner Cable test in Columbus, Ohio, with 30 channels and a wired remote; Vivian Horner's commercial-free preschool Pinwheel channel lived on. Pinwheel became Nickelodeon in 1979, and the rumored link between Talent Search and Star Search was dismissed.

segments.title: Cy Schneider era and early shows
segments.summary: Advertising executive Cy Schneider became Nickelodeon's first president in 1980 and marketed it as the young people's network. Early shows included Reggie Jackson's World of Sports and Leonard Nimoy's Standby... Lights, Camera, Action, and Livewire, a teen current-events show.

segments.title: Geraldine Laybourne and Canadian imports
segments.summary: Geraldine Laybourne shifted the network to find out what kids wanted instead of selling to them. Nickelodeon imported many Canadian shows, including You Can't Do That on Television, created by Roger Price and Jeffrey Darby, whose teen performers had input into scripts.
topics: You Can't Do That on Television

segments.title: Slime origins and the green slime
segments.summary: Discussion of the slime tradition, which began on You Can't Do That on Television; the green slime was an accident, and the final formula was a methyl cellulose blend, after earlier tries with cottage cheese, vegetable oil, pudding, Jello, and applesauce.
topics: You Can't Do That on Television slime

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief transition before the next segment.

segments.title: Bob Pittman, Fred Allen agency, orange logo, and Jive Five bumpers
segments.summary: Bob Pittman, an MTV co-founder, took over the parent company's oversight in 1983 and Laybourne became network head. The Fred Allen agency rebranded the network through focus groups, and Nickelodeon adopted Pantone 021 orange. Animated bumpers by the Jive Five are mentioned.

segments.title: Out of Control, Turkey TV, and dubbed foreign clips
segments.summary: Nickelodeon produced original shows like Out of Control, hosted by Dave Coulier, and Turkey TV, a clip show. The network also used overdubbed foreign kids' clips, such as Danish children's shows.

segments.title: Double Dare and Mark Summers
segments.summary: Double Dare was developed from an idea by Darby for a game show with wacky challenges, hosted by Mark Summers, shot at WHYY in Philadelphia. Physical challenges included egg throwing and the booger-and-nose challenge. The show became a big hit.

segments.title: Nick at Night, Universal Studios, Finders Keepers, and live-action sitcoms
segments.summary: After A&E ended its evening partnership, Nickelodeon launched Nick at Night with classic reruns. The network moved to Universal Studios, and shows like Finders Keepers, Legends of the Hidden Temple, Hey Dude, Salute Your Shorts, Clarissa Explains It All, and Pete and Pete are discussed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Transition before the cartoon era segment.

segments.title: Cartoon era and Ren and Stimpy
segments.summary: Nickelodeon became known for cartoons; Ren and Stimpy, Doug, and Rugrats premiered in 1991. Creator John Kricfalusi ran the first two seasons before being removed for budget and deadline problems. Years later, in 2018, women came forward alleging he sexually abused them as minors; he gave a non-apology and the statute of limitations had passed.

segments.title: Nickelodeon ratings peak and later cartoons
segments.summary: Nickelodeon was the top cable network for 16 years. Hey Arnold, Jimmy Neutron, Avatar: The Last Airbender, and The Legend of Korra are mentioned, with Janet Varney voicing Korra. Rocco's Modern Life is also discussed.

segments.title: SpongeBob SquarePants and Steven Hillenburg
segments.summary: SpongeBob SquarePants, which began in 1999, became the biggest cartoon on television. Creator Steven Hillenburg negotiated a merchandise percentage, and the show has earned large retail revenue.

segments.title: Saima Zergami era and Dan Schneider abuse scandal
segments.summary: Saima Zergami, network head from 2006 to 2018, is criticized for a merchandise policy that deterred creators, turning down Adventure Time, and for failing to protect child actors. Dan Schneider's shows, including The Amanda Show, Drake and Josh, iCarly, and Zoey 101, featured sexual humor, and the hosts discuss abuse by Brian Peck, Jason Handy, and an animator named Ezel Channel.

segments.title: Jeanette McCurdy, Dan Schneider firing, and network decline
segments.summary: Dan Schneider was pushed out after Jeanette McCurdy's allegations; McCurdy's 2022 memoir I'm Glad My Mother's Dead described his conduct. Viacom CBS's investigation found no evidence of sexual misconduct but cited verbal abuse. McCurdy was reportedly offered $300,000 to stay silent, which she refused. Nickelodeon's ratings have dropped to about 122,000 daily viewers.

segments.title: Cable ratings comparison and hotel TV motion smoothing
segments.summary: Hosts compare Nickelodeon's daily viewership to Disney Channel, Cartoon Network, and TV Land, then briefly digress into motion smoothing on hotel TVs and Friends reruns.

segments.title: Transition to listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: rope versus line
segments.summary: A listener named Bill, a former sailor's employee from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, notes that rope becomes line once cut and used on a ship, and Chuck had used the word rope in a Nantucket story.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Credits and closing for the show.
